source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται. τί δ’;
pass_a_gloss: The things following are to be given back and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy is to be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not think of their allegories now as the gnosis hands down the truth, if they show something else, just as the ancient wise men show something else. But they say that God passes through all of existence, we however call Him only the creator and the creator by word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray, 'He passes through and fills all things because of His purity', since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not however one beginning. Let them know therefore the so-called matter, uncreated and unformed, as it is said by them, and let it be said more boldly, not being, in relation to Plato. And not having known the one truly existing beginning in the most mystical way, he says these things in the Timaeus with the same words. Now therefore let our position be as follows: the thing about all things, whether beginning or beginnings or however it seems to them, is not to be said now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to show the things that seem in the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', has given them an opportunity for material existence. For Epicurus, the idea of the automatic did not follow from what was said, and from this, vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. And for Aristotle, providence extended up to the moon from this psalm: 'Lord, your mercy and your truth in the sky, and your truth to the clouds'. For the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the coming of the Lord. And the punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all the poetic muse, but also Greek philosophy, borrowed from barbarian philosophy. For Plato, at the end of his Republic, says with the same words: 'Here indeed wild men, fiery to see, standing, learning the sound, having taken some privately, led them away, but having bound the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, having thrown them down and flayed them, they dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphalathoi'. For the men, the fiery ones, want to signify angels to him, who having taken the unjust, punish them; He who makes, he says, His angels spirits and His servants a burning fire. It follows for them that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What then?

pass_b_english: We must now give back what follows and show more clearly the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they also claim the soul is. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not, however, think of their allegories now as the gnosis hands down the truth, if they show one thing but signal another, just as the ancient wise wrestlers do. But whereas they say that God passes through all of existence, we call him only the creator, the maker by his word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray: "He passes through and fills all things because of his purity" (Wisdom 7:24), since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom created by God. "Yes," they say, "but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings — both the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic — not, however, a single beginning." Let them know, then, the so-called matter, described by them as unqualified and unformed, and let it be said more boldly that it is non-being, according to Plato. And not having known the one truly existing beginning in the most mystical way, he says these things in the Timaeus with those very words. Now, then, let our position be as follows: the question concerning all things, whether there is a beginning or beginnings or however it seems to them, is not to be spoken of now, for no other reason than that it is difficult to declare the things that seem true in the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic utterance, "The earth was invisible and unformed" (Genesis 1:2), has given them an opening for material existence. For Epicurus, the idea of the automatic, failing to follow the text, produced from this vanity of vanities: "All things are vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). And for Aristotle, providence extended only as far as the moon, drawing from this psalm: "Lord, your mercy is in the sky, and your truth reaches to the clouds" (Psalm 36:5). For the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the coming of the Lord. And the punishments after death, the punishment by fire, all the poetic muse, and Greek philosophy as well, borrowed from barbarian philosophy. Plato, at the end of his Republic, speaks with these very words: "Here indeed wild men, fiery to behold, standing by, discerning the sound; taking some privately they led them away, but binding the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, throwing them down and flaying them, they dragged them along the road outside, striking them with thorns." For the fiery men, he says, signify angels who, taking the unjust, punish them; "He who makes his angels spirits and his servants a burning fire" (Psalm 104:4). It follows for them that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, existing in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What then?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Greek syntax and theological distinctions. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version with necessary scripture citations (Wisdom 7:24, Genesis 1:2, Ecclesiastes 1:2, Psalm 36:5, Psalm 104:4) which are required for clarity in patristic texts. The translation of 'ἀσπαλάθων' as 'thorns' in Pass B is a standard rendering for the context of the Republic passage. All clauses, including the nuances of the Stoic/Platonic comparisons and the critique of the 'automatic' in Epicurus, are preserved.

Stromata 14: 'ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν' (Pass A) vs 'ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν' (Pass B) - Pass B incorrectly cites Psalm 36:5 for a phrase that does not match the actual wording of the psalm. The correct reference for 'ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν' is Psalm 36:6, not 36:5.
reasons: scripture: Pass B incorrectly cites Psalm 36:5 for the phrase 'ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν', which does not appear in that verse. The correct reference is Psalm 36:6.
